title: SQL vs NoSQL
subtitle: Choose a data model and storage engine from access patterns and required guarantees
objectives: Say what NoSQL actually means and debunk the speed and schemaless myths
Match the four NoSQL families to the data shapes and access patterns they serve
Explain the deepest difference: model the data vs model the queries
Choose honestly — starting from access patterns and guarantees, not from fashion

exercises.title: NoSQL is an umbrella term for several non-relational data models
exercises.body: NoSQL is a broad industry label covering key-value, document, wide-column, graph, and other non-relational databases. “Not only SQL” is a later expansion of the name, not a capability definition. The label specifies no storage engine, query language, consistency model, or performance profile; each product defines those properties.
exercises.note: Evaluate a specific database and configuration. The NoSQL label alone does not establish transaction support, schema enforcement, durability, or horizontal scalability.

exercises.prompt: An order write updates inventory and payment in two independent stores. Put both records in one relational transaction.
exercises.beforeStatus: CRASH AFTER PAYMENT · payment committed; inventory update missing
exercises.afterStatus: CRASH BEFORE COMMIT · both changes roll back together
exercises.result: The partial order state was eliminated
exercises.why: A transaction inside one database can commit both row changes or roll both back. This does not make an external payment provider part of the same transaction; cross-system effects still require idempotency or a workflow such as an outbox and compensation.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: An order write updates inventory and payment in two independent stores. Put both records in one relational transaction. Place Relational DB, Payment row, Inventory row. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Order service → Relational DB; Relational DB → Payment row; Relational DB → Inventory row. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A transaction inside one database can commit both row changes or roll both back. This does not make an external payment provider part of the same transaction; cross-system effects still require idempotency or a workflow such as an outbox and compensation.

exercises.prompt: What does the modern label 'NoSQL' tell you?
choices: Databases with no query language at all
It is an umbrella label for several non-relational database families; it does not specify one query language or guarantee set
Databases that are always faster than SQL ones
Databases that have no schema
exercises.why: NoSQL is now used as an umbrella label for key-value, document, wide-column, graph, and other non-relational systems. The historical name has been expanded as “not only SQL,” but that phrase is not a technical definition. Many products provide query languages, schemas, and transactions, so evaluate the product's actual data model and guarantees.

exercises.prompt: DynamoDB reads one item by its full partition key; PostgreSQL scans an unindexed column across 50 million rows. Why can the DynamoDB request be faster in this comparison?
choices: Because every NoSQL database is inherently faster
The DynamoDB request uses its designed key access path, while the PostgreSQL query lacks a matching index
Because PostgreSQL cannot look up keys
Because DynamoDB never supports transactions
exercises.why: The named key lookup follows DynamoDB's intended access path, while the unindexed PostgreSQL predicate scans many rows. Adding a suitable PostgreSQL index could reverse or erase the gap. The NoSQL label alone says nothing definitive about joins, transactions, guarantees, or speed.

exercises.prompt: A document database is often called 'schemaless'. So where did the schema go?
choices: There genuinely isn't one — the data has no shape
Into your application code — every reader must now handle every historical shape of the data
Into the operating system
It's generated automatically at runtime
exercises.why: Every document has a schema formed by its fields, value types, and nesting. When the database permits multiple shapes in one collection, application writers validate each shape and readers support every stored version. Schema-on-read therefore requires application-level validation and migration-compatible readers whenever document versions coexist.

exercises.prompt: SQL enforces the shape of data when you ______; many NoSQL stores leave it to be interpreted when you read.
choices: write
delete
connect
backup
exercises.why: Schema-on-write validates a record against declared types and constraints during insertion or update. When shape is interpreted only on read, malformed or older records can remain stored and each reader must recognize or transform them.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are TRUE of relational databases? Select all.
choices: They enforce structure and relationships for you
They're built around joining normalized tables
They cannot handle large scale under any circumstances
They give strong transactional guarantees
exercises.why: Relational databases enforce schemas and relationships, execute joins across normalized tables, and support transactions with configurable isolation. Their scale limit depends on workload and architecture; relational systems can scale vertically, use replicas and partitions, or run as distributed SQL systems.

exercises.prompt: So what's the genuinely useful question when picking a database?
choices: Is it SQL or NoSQL?
What will I ask of this data, what must never be wrong, and what does this database give up?
Which one is newest?
Which one does my favourite company use?
exercises.why: Access patterns determine which reads and writes must be efficient, while required guarantees determine acceptable consistency, isolation, and durability behavior. Comparing those requirements with a database's actual mechanisms is more precise than choosing from its SQL or NoSQL category.

exercises.title: NoSQL data models optimize different access paths
exercises.body: A key-value store maps an exact key to an opaque value. A document store indexes fields inside self-contained records. A wide-column store partitions sparse rows by a partition key and orders them within a partition. A graph store represents vertices and edges for relationship traversal.
exercises.note: Queries outside the store's indexed access path may require a scan, duplicated data, or a separate index. Required query patterns therefore shape the storage model.

exercises.prompt: A product page reads one product plus 30 separately stored attribute rows. Store the read-together document under the product ID.
exercises.result: The storage shape now matches the dominant access pattern
exercises.why: Embedding data that is read and updated as one aggregate removes joins or repeated lookups. It becomes expensive when embedded collections grow without bound or require frequent independent updates.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A product page reads one product plus 30 separately stored attribute rows. Store the read-together document under the product ID. Place Product API, Product document. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Product API → Product document. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Embedding data that is read and updated as one aggregate removes joins or repeated lookups. It becomes expensive when embedded collections grow without bound or require frequent independent updates.

exercises.prompt: Match each NoSQL family to the shape it's built for.

pairs.right: Get/put a value by one key
Huge tables, queried by partition key

exercises.why: Key-value stores optimize lookup by one key; document stores keep self-contained structured records; wide-column stores distribute rows by partition key; graph databases represent vertices and edges for relationship traversal. The distinct data models make each family efficient for different query shapes.

exercises.prompt: You need to store user sessions: looked up only by session id, never queried any other way. Which shape fits?
choices: Key-value
Graph
Wide-column
Relational with 6 tables
exercises.why: A session identifier maps directly to one session value, so a key-value store supports the complete access pattern with a single keyed operation. Its partitioning and indexing can be organized around that key because no joins or secondary predicates are required.

exercises.prompt: User profiles are durable in Postgres and read millions of times per second by user ID. Add a rebuildable serving cache in front of that source of truth.
exercises.why: Redis serves high-volume profile lookups from memory, while every cached value can be rebuilt from the durable Postgres record. The design must define expiration, invalidation, and fallback behavior when Redis misses or fails; Redis is not pretending to hold the only session record.

exercises.prompt: You're storing a product catalog where every type has wildly different attributes — a book has an author, a shirt has a size, a laptop has RAM. Which fits most naturally?
choices: Key-value
Document
Graph
One relational table with 200 mostly-null columns
exercises.why: A document store can represent each product as one self-contained record with fields appropriate to its type, avoiding a very wide sparse table. If the store does not enforce per-type validation, the application must ensure that required fields such as a shirt's size are present.

exercises.prompt: You need 'friends of friends who like X, within 3 hops.' In SQL that's a self-join per hop. What's built for this?
choices: Key-value
Document
Graph
Wide-column
exercises.why: A graph database stores relationships as edges connected to vertices, so a traversal follows adjacent edges at each hop. This directly represents a friends-of-friends query; in a relational model, each additional hop commonly requires another self-join or recursive query step.

exercises.prompt: Cassandra can absorb enormous write volume across many nodes. What's the catch?
choices: There isn't one — it's strictly better
You must know your query patterns up front: tables are designed around the partition key, and ad-hoc queries are painful or impossible
It can't actually write quickly
It only works on one machine
exercises.why: Cassandra distributes rows by partition key and orders data within each partition, so efficient queries must constrain keys that match that layout. A new access pattern may require a separately denormalized table and a backfill because cluster-wide joins and unrestricted scans are not its normal query path.

lessons.title: Model the data vs model the queries

exercises.title: Denormalization precomputes read shapes by duplicating data
exercises.body: Normalized relational data stores each fact once and uses `JOIN` operations to combine related rows at read time. Stores without server-side joins often denormalize: a write copies related fields into records required by a known read path, so that read can use one lookup.
exercises.note: Propagation to duplicated records can fail partway and expose mixed versions. Retries, repair jobs, or version checks must handle incomplete updates.

exercises.prompt: Which contrast best describes normalized join-at-read modeling versus access-path-specific denormalization?
choices: The syntax you type
Normalized designs store facts separately and join them for indexed access paths; denormalized designs duplicate read shapes for known queries
How fast they read from disk
One uses JSON and one doesn't
exercises.why: Normalized designs reduce duplicated facts and reconstruct results at read time, but still need indexes, partitions, and sometimes materialized views for real access patterns. Denormalized designs precompute selected read shapes, trading simpler reads for write amplification and synchronization work.

exercises.prompt: An invoice must preserve the customer's name exactly as it appeared at purchase time and render with one DynamoDB item read. What should the order item store?
choices: Run two queries and join in your app
Duplicate the customer's name into the order record itself
Give up and use SQL
Store a pointer and follow it
exercises.why: Copying the purchase-time name into the order creates the required historical snapshot and satisfies the one-read contract. Looking up the current customer record would change old invoices after a rename. If the product instead required current names, indirection or propagated updates could be valid.

exercises.prompt: The product requires a user's current display name on all 10,000 old posts. You copied that name into every post, and the user renames themselves. What now?
choices: One update — the database handles the rest
You must update 10,000 records, and until you finish, the system displays two different names
Nothing — old posts keep the old name and that's correct
The database refuses the change
exercises.why: Because the requirement says every post shows the current name, propagating the rename requires up to 10,000 writes. During a non-atomic backfill, readers can see mixed versions; indirection, version checks, or repair jobs can change that tradeoff. A historical-name product would intentionally leave old posts unchanged.

exercises.prompt: A feed serves 10,000 reads/sec and 100 fan-out events/sec. Reads must use one keyed lookup; up to 5 minutes of staleness and 20× storage are acceptable, and workers can absorb the amplified writes. Slide toward the storage shape.
exercises.rightLabel: Denormalize (store the answer, pay at write time)
exercises.why: The stated one-lookup read contract, 100:1 read-to-event ratio, tolerated staleness, storage budget, and available workers make precomputed feed records a fit. If freshness were immediate or celebrity fan-out exceeded write capacity, join-at-read or a hybrid design could win despite the same read ratio.

exercises.prompt: What are the real costs of denormalizing? Select all.
choices: Copies can disagree with each other
Writes get more expensive
Reads get slower
You must know your access patterns in advance
exercises.why: Duplicated values can diverge when propagation fails or is delayed, one logical change fans out into more physical writes, and the duplicated layout serves only the access patterns it anticipated. Denormalization generally improves the targeted reads by removing joins or extra lookups.

exercises.prompt: Your NoSQL data model can answer every question your product asks today. What's the risk?
choices: There's no risk — it works
Tomorrow's question may not fit the shape you committed to, and reshaping stored data is far harder than writing a new query
It will run out of disk
It can't be backed up
exercises.why: A query-oriented NoSQL layout encodes its supported access patterns in partition keys, sort keys, indexes, and duplicated views. When a new query cannot use an existing access path, the system needs a new table or index and may need to backfill existing records into that structure.

exercises.title: Cross-partition joins and transactions require network coordination
exercises.body: When related rows occupy different machines, a join must route work to multiple partitions and transfer intermediate results. An atomic transaction spanning those partitions also needs a coordination protocol so participants reach one commit outcome despite delay or failure.
exercises.note: Coordination adds network round trips and ties completion to slow or unavailable participants. Some distributed stores restrict joins or transaction scope to keep operations local.

exercises.prompt: Build one Cassandra write route. The coordinator uses `device_id` to locate a token range, then sends the write to that range's replica set.
exercises.why: A Cassandra coordinator maps the partition key through the partitioner to a token range and forwards the write to replicas responsible for that range, so different keys can spread work across nodes. If one `device_id` becomes hot, all of its writes still target one replica set and can overload it even after unrelated nodes are added.

exercises.prompt: Build the end-to-end path required by this scenario: Build one Cassandra write route. The coordinator uses `device_id` to locate a token range, then sends the write to that range's replica set.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Write → Cassandra Coordinator; Cassandra Coordinator → Partitioner / Token Lookup; Partitioner / Token Lookup → Replica Set for Token Range. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A Cassandra coordinator maps the partition key through the partitioner to a token range and forwards the write to replicas responsible for that range, so different keys can spread work across nodes. If one `device_id` becomes hot, all of its writes still target one replica set and can overload it even after unrelated nodes are added.

exercises.prompt: Which are legitimate reasons to reach for NoSQL? Select all.
choices: One well-known access pattern at massive scale
Data that's naturally self-contained documents
Relational feels old-fashioned
You need writes distributed across many nodes and don't need cross-node transactions
exercises.why: A fixed high-volume key pattern can use purpose-built partitioning, self-contained entities map directly to documents, and distributed writes are simpler when cross-node transactions are unnecessary. Each is a workload requirement that can justify a specific NoSQL model; perceived modernity provides no technical fit.

exercises.prompt: New product. You don't yet know what queries you'll need, and you have 1,000 users. Sane default?
choices: Cassandra, to be ready for scale later
A relational database — flexible about questions you haven't thought of, constraints for free, and far more headroom than you need
MongoDB, because JSON is convenient
A graph database, since everything is connected
exercises.why: With modest current load and uncertain future queries, a relational database provides constraints, transactions, joins, and flexible querying without requiring access-pattern-specific duplication. A distributed store becomes justified when measured workload or availability requirements exceed that architecture's practical limits.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is TRUE about the SQL/NoSQL landscape today?
choices: NoSQL databases never support transactions
The lines have blurred: Postgres stores and indexes JSON, MongoDB added transactions, and NewSQL systems aim for relational semantics with horizontal scale
SQL databases cannot store JSON
The two worlds remain completely separate
exercises.why: Modern products combine features across categories: PostgreSQL can store and index JSON, MongoDB supports multi-document transactions, and distributed SQL systems retain relational semantics across nodes. Product-specific guarantees and limits therefore matter more than the historical label.

exercises.prompt: A team picked NoSQL 'for scale.' A year later they need a report that requires joining across two collections. What happens?
choices: It's trivial — they just write the query
They must denormalize (taking on the update burden), join in application code (slow, N+1), or migrate — the flexibility they gave up is exactly what they now need
The database adds joins automatically
Nothing changes
exercises.why: Without server-side joins, the team must copy data into a query-specific view, issue and combine multiple application queries, or migrate. Application-side joining can cause N+1 requests—one initial query followed by one query per result—and lacks the database optimizer's ability to choose a set-oriented plan.

exercises.prompt: You're storing financial transactions for a bank. Slide toward your choice.
exercises.why: A financial ledger requires enforceable invariants and atomic multi-row changes so debits, credits, and balances cannot partially apply. A relational database is a strong default because it provides constraints and Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability (ACID), though a NoSQL product with equivalent verified guarantees could also qualify.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest way to choose a database?
choices: Pick whatever's trending this year
Start from access patterns and required guarantees; default to relational unless a specific need pushes you off it — and know exactly what you're giving up
Always NoSQL — it's the future
Always SQL — NoSQL is a fad
exercises.why: Access patterns identify required keys, joins, scans, and read/write ratios; correctness requirements identify necessary constraints, transactions, consistency, and durability. A relational default preserves broad query flexibility, while a specific workload may justify accepting a NoSQL system's narrower model or different guarantees.

exercises.prompt: A fraud investigator repeatedly asks for paths between accounts, devices, cards, and IP addresses up to six relationships deep. Which model matches the access pattern?
choices: One CSV file per account
A document store guarantees every multi-hop query is cheap
A graph model with indexed relationships
A key-value lookup with no relationship traversal
exercises.why: The question is a bounded graph traversal across several relationship types. A graph model represents those edges directly; product choice still depends on scale, consistency, and operational constraints.
